evidence: src/domain/stock-allocation-service.ts: reserve() enforces an invariant: every line must have enough stock before any reservation happens, otherwise it throws DomainError('INSUFFICIENT_STOCK'). This is a domain business rule.
src/domain/stock-allocation-service.ts: it depends only on ProductRepository, an interface defined in the domain layer (src/domain/product-repository.ts), not on any concrete persistence technology.
src/domain/stock-allocation-service.ts: no framework, transport, database or serialization code is present.
src/domain/stock-allocation-service.ts: this.products.save(product) goes through an abstract domain port. Whether saving should sit in the application layer is a gray area, not a clear misplacement.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: This file is a domain service that holds business rules. reserve() checks that every line has enough stock before it reserves anything, so the reservation is all-or-nothing, and it throws DomainError("INSUFFICIENT_STOCK") when stock runs short. release() hands stock back. resolve() throws DomainError("NOT_FOUND") when a product is missing. The file uses ProductRepository, an interface defined in the domain layer, through findById and save. It contains no database queries, ORM calls, HTTP/transport handling, framework decorators or configuration. Calling a domain-defined repository port from a domain service is a normal DDD pattern. One could argue that calling products.save() is orchestration that belongs in the application layer, but it only goes through an abstract domain port, so it is not a clear case of a responsibility belonging to another layer. Every responsibility fits the domain layer's role.
